title: What carries across sports
subtitle: Which reliability comparisons are supported across NBA, MLB, soccer and tennis, and what a shared metric scale does not establish
abstract: CourtVision runs the same reliability decomposition and the same skill-score formula in more than one sport, but an identical formula run in two places does not by itself make the two results comparable. kernel_transfer.json (generated 2026-07-22) records five sport/market comparability decisions and marks only two reliability_comparable: mlb moneyline_ingame (n=78,986) and soccer_intl moneyline_ingame (n=9,003), because both score a probability against a resolved binary win/loss outcome on the same 0-1 Murphy reliability scale. The other three are not comparable by construction: mlb totals_margin scores a run-count distribution with CRPS (n=671); nba win-probability stores per-checkpoint Brier means with no reliability split (n=6,371); tennis has no market-side probability at all (n=55,075). Where the comparison is supported the reliability gap has the same sign in both sports, but the two gaps differ by close to 5.9-fold (0.00664 in mlb versus 0.039414 in soccer_intl), and the source file itself calls a two-sport sign match a coincidence worth re-checking, not a pattern. cross_sport_scoreboard.json mixes a Brier-scale family and a CRPS-scale family inside one paired_delta_mean column; its ten mlb_ingame CRPS rows split 7 UNDERPOWERED to 3 MODEL_SHARPER_PROVISIONAL. brier_skill_scores.json returns a BSS below zero against the market at every grain in both sports. The MLB comparisons are withdrawn below pending a corpus regeneration.

blocks.text: CourtVision computes the same two cross-sport statistics in more than one sport: the Murphy reliability component of a Brier score, and the Brier Skill Score (BSS) against a market reference and a climatology reference. Running an identical formula in two sports raises a question before any cross-sport reading: is the result actually comparable, or does it only look comparable because the formula and the numeric scale are the same? kernel_transfer.json exists to answer that row by row.

This paper works through three things in order. First, the five comparability decisions in kernel_transfer.json: two marked reliability_comparable, three not, each with a verbatim reason. Second, cross_sport_scoreboard.json's 17 paired-delta rows, which put one column shape across two different underlying metrics -- Brier for the win-probability rows, CRPS for the margin and total-runs rows. Third, brier_skill_scores.json, where the identical BSS formula runs on populations that differ sharply in size and base rate.

blocks.label: Status
blocks.text: The mlb and soccer_intl moneyline_ingame reliability figures, the mlb_ingame scoreboard rows and the mlb BSS grains below all read the in-game tick corpora. The site's in-game join-integrity finding, measured 2026-09-16, reports 126 of 227 MLB tick files holding ticks from more than one real game and 27,076 of 78,986 ticks sitting in a segment that carries another game's label, so every MLB comparison here is withdrawn pending regeneration of that corpus and is printed as a record of what was published. The comparability decisions themselves -- which axes are shared and which are not -- do not depend on those tick values.

kernel_transfer.json stores one row per sport/market combination under rows[], with fields sport, market, reliability_model, reliability_market, reliability_gap, reliability_unit, reliability_comparable, comparability_reason, verdict, n and sources. Its method field states the file is composition only: reliability and resolution numbers copied verbatim from murphy_decomposition.py and soccer_calibration_pack.py output, verdicts copied or summarized verbatim from each source artifact, nothing recomputed. It carries 5 rows and a generated_at of 2026-07-22T22:55:23Z.

cross_sport_scoreboard.json stores 17 rows (n_rows: 17, generated_at 2026-07-22T20:15:22Z) with fields sport, market, checkpoint, n, paired_delta_mean, paired_delta_95ci and verdict, plus a source path per row. Its method field is the same composition-only statement: every number copied verbatim from its source artifact. The paired_delta_mean column is not one metric -- for the nba and soccer_intl rows it is a Brier-scale delta (from -0.1075 to +0.0019), and for the mlb rows it is a CRPS-scale delta (from -0.0523 to +1.7940). Nothing in the file's schema flags that difference.

brier_skill_scores.json reports the standard BSS formula, BSS = 1 - Brier / Brier_ref, against two references (climatology and market) for mlb (n_rows 78,986, sport_base_rate 0.4563) and soccer_intl (n_rows 9,003, sport_base_rate 0.6055). Its floors field states a rule for itself, n>=30 rows per grain before a BSS is reported, and every grain listed carries below_floor: false. generated_at is 2026-07-25T11:12:35Z.

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.text: kernel_transfer.json marks a row reliability_comparable only when both sides score a probability against a resolved binary outcome using the Murphy reliability component on the same 0-1 probability scale -- reliability_unit is literally the string brier_reliability_component (probability scale, 0-1) for both comparable rows. Sharing that scale says the two numbers are measured the same way, and nothing about the corpus, the outcome type, or the games they were measured on.

Every number below is copied from kernel_transfer.json, cross_sport_scoreboard.json or brier_skill_scores.json; none is re-scored. Three quantities are computed here, each trivial arithmetic on cited fields: the ratio of mlb to soccer_intl corpus size (78,986 / 9,003, about 8.8), the share of each sport's named brier_skill_scores.json grains that sum to its own all grain, and the ratio of the two comparable reliability_gap values (0.039414 / 0.00664), which kernel_transfer.json's own reliability_transfer_summary already states as about 5.9x and this paper quotes rather than recomputing.

The verdict labels quoted throughout (UNDERPOWERED, MARKET_SHARPER_PROVISIONAL, MODEL_SHARPER_PROVISIONAL, REPLICATED, REJECT) are copied verbatim from the source files' own verdict and comparable_groups fields; this paper does not re-run the underlying tests.

rows: not applicable -- CRPS, no reliability axis
blocks.note: yes/no reproduces the reliability_comparable field verbatim; the gap is reliability_model minus reliability_market as stored, not recomputed.

items: Both comparable rows (mlb and soccer_intl moneyline_ingame) share one reason, given verbatim: both sides are Brier scores of a probability against a binary win/loss outcome -- the reliability component is on the same 0-1 probability scale in both sports, the one honest cross-sport axis here.
mlb totals_margin (n=671), not comparable: CRPS scores a full run-count distribution, not a binary outcome probability -- Murphy reliability/resolution is undefined for it here.
nba winprob_ingame (n=6,371), not comparable: nba's benchmark stores per-checkpoint Brier MEANS only -- no 10-bin Murphy reliability/resolution split has been computed locally for nba win-prob.

tennis pregame_prior + ingame_surface_gate (n=55,075), not comparable: both tennis gate receipts are model-vs-model checks -- no market_prob to decompose against, reliability undefined by construction.

blocks.text: Where the comparison is supported, the reliability_gap agrees in sign: the model is less reliable than the market in both mlb (+0.00664) and soccer_intl (+0.039414), each stored as reliability_model minus reliability_market. The two gaps differ by close to 5.9-fold, and kernel_transfer.json's own reliability_transfer_summary is explicit that two sports is not enough to call this a general cross-sport pattern -- a same-direction coincidence worth re-checking if a third sport gets a market-side Murphy decomposition, not a claim. This paper offers no explanation for either the sign match or the magnitude difference.

blocks.note: Verdict labels copied verbatim from the file. CRPS-scale rows (mlb_ingame, mlb_pregame) and Brier-scale rows (nba, soccer_intl) are not on the same numeric axis -- see the caution below.

blocks.label: Caution
blocks.text: Two different metrics share one column in this table. paired_delta_mean is a Brier-scale delta for the nba and soccer_intl winprob rows (-0.1075 to +0.0019) and a CRPS-scale delta for the mlb rows (-0.0523 to +1.7940). CRPS and Brier are not the same unit -- kernel_transfer.json's comparability_reason for mlb totals_margin states CRPS is undefined on the Murphy Brier axis used elsewhere here. Treating the mlb CRPS delta of 1.7940 as a larger effect than the nba Brier delta of -0.0084 establishes only that the two are on different scales.

Within a metric family, most rows do not resolve in either direction. All four nba winprob checkpoints and the mlb_pregame row are labeled UNDERPOWERED or MARKET_SHARPER_PROVISIONAL, and the ten mlb_ingame CRPS rows split 7 UNDERPOWERED to 3 MODEL_SHARPER_PROVISIONAL -- the split kernel_transfer.json's own mlb totals_margin row states verbatim as "MODEL_SHARPER_PROVISIONAL: 3, UNDERPOWERED: 7". The three MODEL_SHARPER_PROVISIONAL rows are consecutive mlb_ingame total_runs checkpoints (end_inning_6, n=54; end_inning_7, n=55; end_inning_8, n=49), each still marked PROVISIONAL rather than settled. nba's one resolved row, end_q1 (n=1,592, paired_delta_mean -0.0084, CI -0.0161 to -0.0008), is MARKET_SHARPER_PROVISIONAL.

A verdict in this file is not a reading of the interval printed beside it. cross_sport_scoreboard.json's method field states that every value is copied verbatim from the artifact named in rows[].source, so the support rule that produced each label lives in that upstream benchmark, not in the interval column. That is why a support rule and an interval excluding zero can coexist: mlb_ingame home_margin|end_inning_5 (n=26, CI 0.3259 to 1.4888) and the two soccer_intl rows (n=22, CI -0.1570 to -0.0336; n=17, CI -0.1885 to -0.0316) each carry an interval excluding zero and each read UNDERPOWERED. The label says whether the benchmark judged that checkpoint supported enough to name a direction; the interval says where the paired delta sat. Reading the two as if they had to agree misreads the column.

sections.heading: Results: the same BSS formula in two sports

blocks.text: Table 3 gives the BSS-vs-market figures for every grain brier_skill_scores.json reports, in both sports it covers.

blocks.caption: Brier Skill Score vs market by sport and grain, all 11 reported grains (source brier_skill_scores.json, generated 2026-07-25)
blocks.note: Do not rank the all row against its sport's named grains: all is the full corpus, not a sum of the named grains. Below floor reproduces the file's own below_floor field.

blocks.text: BSS against market is negative at every one of the 11 grains listed, in both sports -- from -0.0794 (mlb, early) to -0.4635 (mlb, late), and from -0.4701 (soccer_intl, 60-75) to -1.0794 (soccer_intl, 0-15). Every grain carries below_floor: false. Both sports run the identical formula against the identical kind of reference and both return a negative number nearly everywhere, but the populations are not alike: mlb's all grain has 78,986 rows against soccer_intl's 9,003 (about 8.8 times), the base rates differ (0.4563 against 0.6055), and the named grains cover 66.6 percent of mlb rows against 40.6 percent of soccer_intl rows.

Running the same formula on two populations of very different size, base rate and grain coverage is where a shared scale does not establish a shared population. The negative-against-market result is kept as the honest outcome in both sports, but the difference is why this paper reports two separately measured, same-direction results rather than one combined finding.

sections.heading: Robustness and what would falsify this

items: If a third sport gained a market-side Murphy reliability decomposition and its reliability_gap sign disagreed with mlb and soccer_intl, the current sign-agrees-across-two-sports reading would have to be dropped, exactly as kernel_transfer.json's own summary warns.

Verdict labels and confidence intervals are separate columns in cross_sport_scoreboard.json: the labels are copied verbatim from the upstream benchmark named in rows[].source, so if that benchmark's support rule changed, rows whose interval already excludes zero could change label with no new measurement. Neither column can be used to check the other.
If the three mlb_ingame total_runs MODEL_SHARPER_PROVISIONAL checkpoints (n=49-55) reversed sign at a larger n, reading that run as a stable in-game pattern would have to be dropped.

If soccer_intl's BSS-vs-market figures moved into mlb's range (roughly -0.08 to -0.46) on a larger soccer_intl corpus, the current gap between the two sports' BSS levels would have to be re-read; at the sizes published here this paper attributes that gap to nothing.
Only 2 of the 5 kernel_transfer.json rows support any cross-sport reliability comparison; the other 3 are excluded by construction, not measured and found equal.
The reliability_gap sign match rests on two sports; kernel_transfer.json's own reliability_transfer_summary calls it a coincidence worth re-checking, not a pattern.

cross_sport_scoreboard.json mixes a Brier-scale metric family and a CRPS-scale metric family inside one paired_delta_mean column; comparing raw magnitudes across that boundary is not supported by the file.

Verdict labels in cross_sport_scoreboard.json are copied verbatim from the upstream benchmark named in rows[].source, not derived from the interval beside them, so a row can carry an interval excluding zero and still read UNDERPOWERED; this paper reports the labels as published and does not re-derive them.

brier_skill_scores.json's named grains do not sum to each sport's all row (66.6 percent of mlb rows, 40.6 percent of soccer_intl rows), so the per-grain and all-row figures describe overlapping but not identical sets of games.
None of the three artifacts tests why the market is more reliable than the model; a measured gap is reported, not a mechanism.
The MLB comparisons here read the in-game tick corpus the site's join-integrity finding records as partly mislabelled, so they are withdrawn pending its regeneration.

sections.heading: How to read this on the site

blocks.text: The cross-sport-comparability inspector is built directly on kernel_transfer.json and is the place to check, before reading any number across sports, whether a sport/market pair is one of the two marked reliability_comparable. The score-decomposition inspector carries the Murphy detail for those two rows, and the calibration inspector the per-grain BSS context behind Table 3.

Table 2's scoreboard and the figure above are one view of the same paired-delta rows the cross_sport_scoreboard module renders directly; check whether a sport/market pair is comparable first, then read its scoreboard or BSS numbers. Read the in-game join-integrity finding before taking any MLB row here as current.

limitations: Only 2 of the 5 kernel_transfer.json rows support any cross-sport reliability comparison; the other 3 are excluded by construction, not measured and found equal.
The reliability_gap sign match between mlb and soccer_intl rests on n=2 sports; kernel_transfer.json's own summary calls it a coincidence worth re-checking, not a pattern.

cross_sport_scoreboard.json mixes a Brier-scale metric family and a CRPS-scale metric family inside one paired_delta_mean column; comparing raw magnitudes across that boundary is not supported by the file.
Two soccer_intl scoreboard rows (n=17, n=22) have confidence intervals that exclude zero yet carry an UNDERPOWERED verdict, and the file does not document the labeling rule.

brier_skill_scores.json's named grains do not sum to each sport's all row (66.6 percent of mlb rows, 40.6 percent of soccer_intl rows), so grain-level and all-level figures describe overlapping but not identical row sets.
None of the three artifacts here tests why the market is more reliable, or has better resolution, than the model in mlb and soccer_intl; a measured gap is reported, not a mechanism.
